comment_content:
1. Association

This course introduces common algorithms used in data science. You will learn to compute the algorithms like a computer. I don't understand the meaning of learning them as the computers are already performing these functions.
The course also briefly introduces a popular topic neural network, which is related to AI.
comment_teaching:
Professor is quite nice. He answers student's questions after class or through email. His lesson focuses on examples. However, his lecture slides are not useful for revision.
The gives out coupons during lesson if you answer his questions. The coupons can be used to either obtain full marks for one question in an assignment or obtain full marks for prediction in the project. It's not difficult to get a coupon.
comment_grading:
Midterm mean score, final -0.4 SD, assignments, projects and attendance full marks, eventually got a B.
To be honest, the grading is good enough given the exam scores. However, personally speaking, I'm not satisfied with the score as I spent quite a lot of time learning and revising course contents, and the grade does not reflect my effort in this course. Computer Science and Math students pull up the average so much that other students struggle to reach the mean.
The exam papers obviously include easy questions and difficult questions. The examples given during lectures are rather easy but exam questions are much more complicated. The easy ones you just need to apply the algorithm taught during lesson and you can get the marks. For the difficult questions, they are REALLY difficult. Even after Raymond's explanation, I still have no idea how that can be solved.
comment_workload:
As mentioned in the grading section, I spent quite a lot of time in learning and revising course materials. It is essential to attend the lessons or watch the recordings, as the slides are missing many key concepts and steps of the algorithm.
There are two assignments, each includes 5 questions. You can complete the assignments following the examples during lecture.
For the project, you can form a group of two or just on your own. I did the project on my own and there isn't any problem with that. You will be given a training set, and you have to predict the target attribute for the test set. You need to propose 5 models to do the prediction and submit the results. The main workload lies in the project report, which you need to state the result and findings. The project is quite time consuming.

comment_teaching:
Raymond is one of the best instructors I met in UST. Others have wrote a lot about this, so I want to focus on his coupon system:
A coupon is given to a student whenever he/she answers a question in class. It can be used to waive 1 (out of 5) questions in a homework (there are 2 homeworks and each time you can only use 1 coupon), or guarantee full mark in the output file of project phase 3. Therefore you can use a maximum of 3 coupons throughout the course.
During the first month, a lot of people will raise up their hands each time Raymond asks a question, so it is not so easy to get a coupon from him at that time. However, don't be discouraged. As time passes, it will become less competitive. He will begin giving coupons for participating in in-class activities or some simple questions like "do you remember your instructor's name".
Even if you can't get all 3 coupons, it is good to get at least one for the project as that part of the project is 4% of your grade. Meanwhile, one question in a homework is 1%.

The project can be done on your own or in a 2-person group. I did it in a group but I think the workload is reasonable even if you do it individually. One thing to note is that the instructions are not very clear so make sure you talk to Raymond and the TAs to know what they expect you to write in the project report.

Topic 2 and 3 are same as COMP2211. These topics introduce different models that observe the pattern of some data and make predictions, it shows you how artifical intelligence works. comment_workload:
This is my own subjective opinion only, because my experience in video editing is little to none :p
The workload for this course is extremely intense, if you're not familiar with video editing beforehand, and are aiming to get good grades. For each of the submissions, you have to make a 1~2 minute video (2~3 for the final project), and a commentary video on what you have created. Basically:
-You better have some creative ideas, and don't be afraid to express them. Otherwise, picking the right topic for each video may be quite exhausting & time-consuming!
-The professor values the level of detail in your videos quite a bit, stuff like matching the BGM frame-by-frame, how you apply greenscreen/other techniques to make the video that much funnier/realistic...so if you want to get the good scores, prepare to work sleeplessly/over a few days on the videos : ) I didn't sleep AT ALL the day before each submission.
-Get yourself a teammate. The work can be done by a group of 2, so find a friend & you'll half the workload. I sure relied on my friend quite a bit, couldn't have gotten this far without my bro. (Sike, both of us still went sleepless working on it, so yeah)
-The main video is important, but the commentary may be even more important. The commentary can be a pretty fun video filled with memes or a bit more serious (like an actual commentary), but whatever your style is, you'll want to pick out some of the most important/overlooked details from the main video & explain how those moments were made, instead of just replaying the entire video with some subtitles going over it :p
TL;DR, if you want to enjoy a common core with light workload, this is NOT the place for you. If you like video editing & are willing to either spend 15~20+ hours on each assignment on average, or is OK with getting a lower grade, then this will be a fun course for ya :)

course_name: Creative Sound and Video Design
comment_content:
3 assignments and 1 final project. The first assignment is making a mash-up of the audio from one source with the video of another. The second is using green-screen techniques to combine characters from different media into one setting. The third is making a music video mashup incorporating elements from multiple songs or remixing a given song. The final project is basically do whatever you want, there are no rules (except be really creative). Each submission requires a 1-2 minute video of your work, and a corresponding 1-2 minute commentary video describing your creative and technical choices (except the final project, which is 2-3 minutes for both the video + commentary). You can work on the video yourself or in groups of 2 people (if you want to have a more manageable workload highly recommend you find someone to work with). 
I can totally see people submitting the same types of content for all 4 assignments, as the criteria for all of them were pretty loose and are generally quite friendly towards whatever your passions or interests are.
comment_teaching:
A course that rewards those who self-learns everything and/or already have a developed hobby in music and video making.
Almost no in-class teaching was done. Prof. Horner does enthusiastically go over other people's creations (from this semester + previous semesters) in class and gives out a lot of artistic and a few technical suggestions, but these largely do not really help that much beyond video ideation. The comments he gives you after you submit your video are all just positive remarks like "Great techniques!" or "Amazing idea!", don't expect to receive actual feedback for your video (courtesy of the TA's) until after your video is shown and peer-reviewed.
Other people previously claimed that there were tutorials provided which help students who don't have that much experience get started. My opinion is that this is only to a small extent; these tutorials aren't really that helpful if you want to really impress them and get a decent grade, they either just suggest a few techniques and tools or they're way too esoteric for most people to understand, and many of them really are only for one purpose (ex. they provided a lot of deepfake AI tool tutorials for the final project, which wouldn't be that useful if you don't want to do something like that). Especially noteworthy if you aren't coming from a field or profession where sound/video design is researched or video editing is used, or you aren't a graphics design major at heart, most of the tutorials also use apps and features which either are pretty finicky to use or turns out are behind a paywall. In fact, in my opinion it is really difficult to obtain a decent grade in this course without spending several hundred dollars on video and audio editing software/AI tools (ex. video editing tools: Final Cut Pro is a one-off 2300 HKD purchase, the standard subscription for Capcut premium is 60 HKD/month which you have to purchase to do literally anything (seriously, even splitting audio and video from a clip requires Capcut premium), Davinci Resolve is free but most advanced techniques besides plugins require a subscription that costs 230 HKD/month, the full range of adobe software requires at least a 400 HKD/month subscription to use etc., iMovie is free to use if you have a Mac but I do NOT recommend it for this course as it is so basic and there are so little features). 
Of course, you could have a really creative premise that compensates a lack of technology with either a really good storyline or clever artistic choices, but this is HARD to do especially without making it look or sound like it's "low-budget".
As I am only taking this to complete my last Broadening CC requirement and I have some basic experience in video editing (due to some random stuff i did for a university club a few years ago), the only two subscriptions I purchased was a standard plan for Runway ML (so I could survive assignment 2) and Capcut Premium, both of which I swiftly cancelled after I finished my final project (Audacity, GarageBand (for Mac users), and the base version of Davinci Resolve were free). Even then, I had to rely on my experience on playing an instrument for several years and having a decent knowledge in music theory for assignment 3 and the final project to get a good grade. I recommend you take this course if you're already passionate in video editing and music creation and have or know how to use several of the tools recommended by this course, if not RUN AWAY.

comment_workload:
4 video projects only, seems light right?
NO.
Firstly, the assignment due dates are absolutely atrocious. Assignment 1 due in the middle of add/drop period, assignment 2 right before midterm period, assignment 3 in the middle of midterm period, final project right after midterms end. I constantly found working on these videos got in the way of a ton of other stuff I was doing (for a year 4 student working on postgraduate/job applications, and I anticipate most people taking this course is year 4 given how fast COMP1943 turns from available to waitlist during the first day of course reg, this is borderline hellish).

Prof. Horner and his TA's value quantity AND quality, videos that approach the 2 (or 3) minute limit and are full of artistic details and techniques. Even if you spent a massive amount of time and energy on your assignment, or you have a really good idea, they won't judge you on your idea alone if it looks like you had trouble achieving what you wanted to do.
Don't sleep on the commentary video either, to get a higher grade its not really that suggested to just add subtitles to a running clip of your workspace, instead a separate edited video that explains every important thing you did. The first two assignments I just added subtitles to a video recording of my Capcut workspace for my commentary (because I ran out of time) and neither were received very well. Some people went above and beyond and made their commentary video seemingly more amusing and detailed than their actual assignment, especially if their original video revolves around a theme/subject that isn't very well known by many people (ex. certain sports like F1 or football), but this obviously takes a lot of time. 
(also, quick PSA but please do not just throw a ton of prompts into GenAI tools and make slop videos, it gets extremely boring and repetitive after several watches)
I only spent around 8 hours working on Assignment 1, as the prompt wasn't too difficult to achieve and I already knew before the class began what I wanted to do. However, I had to spend almost 20 hours for Assignment 2 to learn Davinci Resolve, masking, green screen etc., and the TA's still thought my video was pretty mediocre. To make up for this, I spent a bit more time (~25 hours) composing and remixing the song for my Assignment 3, which paid off. Finally, I spent around 30 hours total for the final project making both my audio and video components. This course ain't for you if you don't have any free time or if you value your sleep schedule (although during midterm season most people probably don't value it anyways), I had to pull near all-nighters for these assignments.

Wow-factor of creation video (and behind-the-scenes video), count out of 5:

1/5: Uninspired

comment_grading:
The grading scheme is a ridiculous patchwork: Participation (attendance) 15%, Quizzes 10% (four at 2.5% each), AI news presentation 5% (individual), Reading response 15% (individual) plus 5% peer review, Case study analysis 15% (individual) plus 5% peer review, Debate (group) 15%, and Debate review (individual) 15%, total 100%. 
Anything that has a peer review means that 20% of that item’s weight comes from an anonymous classmate while the TA accounts for the other 80%, so your final mark on a task can be dragged down by one random student’s whim. For example, if the TA gives you 10/15 but a classmate gives 5/15, your weighted score suddenly becomes 9/15. They say you can appeal anonymous reviews only for “obvious inconsistency” or “unreasonable/unrelated” comments, but who decides what’s unreasonable?
These tiny percentages seem insignificant on their own, but they pile up and can wreck your final grade. I was pretty much average on everything (except the debate, where my team got crushed because one single "smart" person hogged two minutes in the free-debate slot and half our team score evaporated), and even being near the mean didn’t spare me from the system’s hair-trigger penalties.
comment_workload:
The grading scheme is a mess. Tons of little sections and one real pain: a formal debate. Yep, an actual timed debate with multiple speakers. In the free-debate bit everyone gets 5 minutes total, but you must swap every ~30 seconds. If your teammate can’t read a timer and hogs 2+ minutes in one turn, congratulations! You just lost half the 15% debate mark.
Quizzes are “open book” but you get only 10 minutes. Three questions are based on a ~10‑page PDF and expect quick, precise answers; the fourth asks you to respond to a Netflix documentary shown in class. Good luck doing that well in 10 minutes.
There’s also a 30-minute “news” presentation at the start of many lectures that must cover AI news from the previous 14 days only. If you present on Nov 20, you can only use items from Nov 6 - 19, which makes finding relevant AI news a matter of luck some weeks.
This is treated as a common-core course, but the workload and micro-requirements feel totally inappropriate and needlessly strict.

comment_content:
I may be biased as I was taught under Mr. Leung's teaching, but the content was not too difficult. The topics taught were:
Logic, Combinations, Probability, Number Theory, Algorithms, Graphs
In terms of difficulty, (in my opinion) they would be arranged (from easiest to hardest)
Logic < Graphs < Algorithms < Number Theory < Combinations < Probability 
The topics taught in:
Logic-- are relatively easy, just make sure not to make careless mistakes for these questions
Graphs-- are mostly "proof" questions. They won't ask you much about graph theory as it will be discussed more in year 3
Algorithms-- understand clearly what big O,theta, and omega are, and you're good to go
Number Theory questions are usually about decrypting texts and stuff like that, which are things that you can memorise. So these questions are practically free marks (unless you're careless)
Combinations and Probability-- now these questions are always tricky. A particular TA named Arman always creates creative and tricky questions. You cannot do these questions through sheer memorisation. You have to use your brain and aimlessly think of methods, which is why it is the hardest.
Comp2711 has a telegram group where you can ask questions to the TAs, and usually get an instant response, which I love.
comment_teaching:
I find Kenneth Leung's teachings to be very interesting. He is always very happy when he discusses the topics at hand. me: total is around 98%, I will change “grading” into E if I don’t get A+. I’m not here to flex and I genuinely hope you guys can all do better than me, so good luck.

comment_teaching: This lecturer is quite helpful as he actually teaches the content and explains the hard sections of the content. He would use whiteboard to draw diagrams to help us visualize the complex knowledge to ease it. Whenever we have questions, he would also answer the questions and address the needs of the students.
comment_grading: The professors are lenient on grading as some may have missed the first few exercises due to add/drop period, and they would allow late submissions and still count the scores. Other than that, the homeworks are also promptly graded, which is decent.
comment_workload: This course has quite a heavy workload as the materials are taught in a fast manner such that there is loads of self-study needed. course_name: Discrete Mathematical Tools for Computer Science
comment_content: The course content covers core knowledge points including logic and proof, sets, functions, algorithms, counting, induction, recursion, probability theory, and graph theory. In addition, the course introduces propositional logic and the use of truth tables, which strengthen students’ ability to reason and construct rigorous arguments. This course has weak relevance to calculus, and the logical thinking it cultivates is of great help to the development of problem-solving skills in subsequent programming learning.
comment_teaching: The instructor explains the concepts in detail, emphasizing both theoretical understanding and practical applications. The teaching pace is moderate, and in-class examples are provided to reinforce comprehension. However, the in-class exercises are sometimes repetitive, focusing more on basic skills rather than challenging applications. Moreover, the results of in-class exercises are counted toward the final grade.
comment_grading: The grading scheme is relatively clear, consisting of homework, quizzes, a midterm, and a final exam. The exam difficulty is moderate, primarily testing fundamental understanding and basic problem-solving skills rather than highly complex questions. Overall, students who keep up with the course should be able to achieve good grades.
comment_workload: Each class includes in-class exercises that must be submitted on the same day. These exercises help students consolidate what they have learned, but may pose some pressure for those with weaker mathematical backgrounds. The professor has mentioned that they will try to help such students “survive” the exams. [However, if you are not good at mathematics or have weak logical thinking skills, this course is definitely not as easy as you might imagine.]

comment_content:
The course covers the same topics as in a regular semester (they didn't even skip graph theory like they did in the spring semester). But the homeworks and exams are extremely easy compared to that of normal semester. So it might be less preferable to someone who prefers rigor. But I assume those guys will take 2711H anyways. 
Although there are many topics, they are very introductory and don't go much in depth (though the questions can be quite challenging), so you would likely need to take other courses such as MATH 4141, MATH 3121, and MATH 2421 to gain a deeper understanding. I believe there is significant overlap with MATH 2421, so if you are a DSCT, COSC, or just a student interested in these subjects, you should definitely consider taking them together.
One interesting finding: The syllabus is an exact copy of UC Berkeley's Math 55 https://math.berkeley.edu/courses/overview/lowerdivcourses/math55
 This is actually a good thing since UCB is known for being a strong CS school, and I don't mind because I don't have to pay $60,000(USD) per year and can still learn the same content.
comment_teaching:
On the first day of lecture, I remember Professor Tai saying, "I have taught this course 10 times," so my expectations were quite high. Unfortunately, they fell short. She struggles with pacing her lectures, frequently stumbles over words, and as a result, might skip crucial parts if she runs out of time or takes an extra 10 minutes to finish.
If it weren’t for the in-class quizzes, I would have only attended the tutorials. In fact, I highly recommend attending all tutorials led by Arman. He is clearly passionate about the subject, provides key insights, and emphasizes intuition in his explanations. He might also drop occasional hints about questions that could appear on exams (as he did for the midterms) during the tutorials.

I am writing this review just after taking my final exam, so the final results haven't been released yet (I’ll update this later if I remember). There will be some exchange students also taking this course, so the mean might not accurately reflect the true UST average. Still, it’s quite competitive to score above +1 SD, as indicated by the high standard deviation and self-selection bias (students who choose to take a course during summer vacation may be more motivated than the general population, but that's just my guess).
Midterms:
    Mean: 60.84
    Median: 61
    High: 99
    Upper Quartile: 82.5
    Low: 0
    Lower Quartile: 41
While these scores might seem high compared to a normal semester, the questions were also significantly easier. The true UST mean (if you exclude exchange students) might have been 65+.
Note: I don't hold any prejudice against exchange students; they often spend less time studying and don't stress about grades as much as UST students, since they want to explore Hong Kong.
For this semester, more weight was given to quizzes, but the way the professor conducted them was less than satisfactory. For instance, she would allocate only 3 minutes for some questions that clearly required 5+ minutes of calculations. Additionally, some students skipped lectures and relied on friends to notify them when quizzes would be held. I noticed this because one time there were only 38 students in the class, yet 44 respondents after the quiz ended (simple pigeonhole principle). Given how quickly some students submitted their quizzes and got 100, I suspect they used ChatGPT, which is clearly unfair since quizzes are worth 18% of the grade.
comment_workload: I believe the workload in the summer semester is lighter, as the homework, midterms, and finals are much easier. So, it really depends on the grade you’re aiming for.

course_name: Discrete Mathematical Tools for Computer Science
comment_content:
The following key topics are taught:
- Propositional Logic: Including operators, equivalences, proofs using laws (without truth tables), and rules of inference.
- Predicate Logic: Including quantifiers (∀, ∃), expressing statements with predicates, negation of quantified statements, and formal proofs.
- Sets and Functions: Including set operations (intersection, union, complement, subsets), proofs (direct and contrapositive), countability/uncountability of sets (e.g., natural numbers, functions from N to N, binary strings), and bijections.
- Counting Principles: Including permutations, combinations, binomial coefficients, arrangements with restrictions (e.g., adjacency, no two alike adjacent), unordered pairs, palindromes, and paths in graphs (without reusing edges).
- Combinatorial Proofs: Proving identities using combinatorial reasoning (e.g., involving subsets and distinct elements).
- Inclusion-Exclusion Principle: Applied to counting problems (e.g., digits in numbers with specific constraints).
- Pigeonhole Principle: Applied to grid-based problems (e.g., colored cells sharing corners).
- Probability: Including basic probabilities, binomial distributions, and scenarios with independent events (e.g., catching flies).
- Random Variables: Including expectation (E), variance (var), linearity of expectation, independence, and comparisons (e.g., E(X^2) vs. E(XY) for dice rolls).
- Graphs
- MOD
- Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT)

3. Don't simply print all powerpoint slides. Try to summarize the content in the slides as your own note documents and print your own note during final. It helps you to have better understandings on concepts and reduce the number of pages of your notes.

comment_content: The course is mainly based on Principles of Microeconomics (10th edition) by N. Gregory Mankiw, published by South-Western, Cengage Learning. The material itself is very basic microeconomics. The lectures do not strictly follow the order of the textbook, and by the end of the semester we roughly reached the chapter on monopoly. That said, as a core business school requirement, you do not really have a choice about whether to take it or not.
comment_teaching:
Li Xuan’s lecturing is honestly not very effective. She tends to look down while speaking, and although her pronunciation is fine, her pauses and sentence breaks can be quite confusing during lectures. However, her understanding of the subject is strong. When you ask questions after class, she explains concepts very clearly and in a fairly intuitive way. The issue is more about in-class delivery than ability.
In contrast, Victor’s tutorials are very well structured. He does a great job highlighting the key points, walking through examples step by step, and making the logic behind each concept very clear. Concept comparisons and distinctions are explained thoroughly. After the first midterm, I stopped going to lectures and only attended tutorials. My personal approach was to go through the lecture material on my own and then rely on tutorials, which turned out to be quite efficient for me.

comment_workload:
The workload is relatively light. There are ten problem sets in total. If you complete them on your own, each usually takes around 1.5 to 2.5 hours, depending on your background. Of course, if you simply look up answers online, half an hour is probably enough. Personally, I do not think the problem sets are very helpful for the final exam.
Both midterms are multiple-choice. Before the exams, I did as many past paper questions as I could find, probably over two hundred in total, which helped a lot with exam familiarity. The final includes both multiple-choice and written questions, and there are no past papers available. My approach was to use AI to generate concept comparison questions, since Li Xuan’s exam style is quite textbook-based and focuses heavily on definitions, concepts, and some logical extensions. The written questions are relatively challenging. My suggestion is to fully understand the provided sample questions. Even though the actual exam questions are not very similar, working through the samples helps you get used to the question types.
